Case study · Delivery & Technology · Roadmapping, Planning & OKRs

Three Sentences, Four Audiences

Bunyaad Clinical Systems and the FY28 roadmap · Hyderabad, Sunday 7 March 2027

1. The night before

At a quarter past eleven on Sunday night, Vikram Sundaresan had three documents open side by side on the same screen, and the problem was that they were the same document. In the first window sat the board pre-read for Monday morning, page nine of which carried the FY28 product plan. In the second sat the deck for Tuesday's Customer Advisory Board in Mumbai, where the chief information officers of eleven hospital groups would spend a day in a conference room in Bandra Kurla Complex being told what Bunyaad Clinical Systems intended to build for them. In the third sat a half-finished web page — bunyaad.in/roadmap — which the company had committed to refresh by Friday, because Bhaskar Research Advisory's submission window for its Asia-Pacific hospital-platform evaluation closed on 19 March and roadmap transparency carried a tenth of the score.

All three documents contained the same three sentences. Bunyaad would ship consent-manager compliance under the Digital Personal Data Protection rules. Bunyaad would ship ambient clinical documentation, the feature that wrote a doctor's notes from the consultation itself. Bunyaad would ship version two of its claims exchange connector. Vikram had written those sentences himself, in a state of some satisfaction, eleven days earlier.

Dr Meenakshi Rao, who had co-founded the company and still ran it, had sent him a single line at nine that evening: Whatever we publish Friday, I want to be able to say the same thing to Laukik on Monday and to the CIOs on Tuesday without changing a word. Can we? He had not yet replied.

2. How Bunyaad came to be shaped this way

Bunyaad Clinical Systems was founded in Hyderabad in 2016 by Dr Meenakshi Rao, a paediatric intensivist who had spent nine years watching nurses transcribe vitals onto paper charts at three in the morning, and Joel D'Souza, an engineer she met through a hospital automation pilot. Their product was unglamorous and deep: an electronic medical record with operating-theatre scheduling, pharmacy and inventory, and insurance claims, sold to the mid-market hospital chains that sit below Apollo, Fortis, Manipal and Narayana Health — fifty to four hundred beds, two to fifteen facilities, a chief information officer who reports to the chief financial officer and has no budget for failure.

By the close of FY26 the company had reached ₹184 crore in revenue, 1,140 employees, 62 hospital groups and 310 live facilities, with engineering in Pune and Hyderabad, design in Berlin, a data and AI team in Toronto, customer success run out of Singapore for everything east and west of India, and a four-person sales office in New Jersey opened in 2026 to chase American physician groups.

One decision from 2022 shapes everything in this case. Bunyaad was then competing for Lagan Hospitals Group, a Pune-headquartered chain of nineteen facilities across Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh, and Lagan's board would not put patient records on shared infrastructure. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act had not yet passed; nobody knew what data residency would come to mean; and Lipi Health Cloud, the Chennai competitor, was multi-tenant and losing every conversation with a nervous hospital trust. Bunyaad chose single tenancy. Every customer would get its own instance, its own database, its own upgrade window, scheduled by its own IT and clinical governance committee, revalidated facility by facility because a hospital cannot take a pharmacy module down on a Tuesday.

The decision won Lagan, and then it won the segment. It also meant that from 2022 onward the sentence "we have shipped it" and the sentence "you have it" described events up to a year apart, and that nobody at Bunyaad owned the distance between them.

3. The industry

Indian hospital software in 2027 is being reorganised from outside by public infrastructure. The Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission has made ABHA identifiers, the Health Facility Registry and the Health Professional Registry the assumed plumbing of any credible system; the National Health Claims Exchange has begun to standardise what used to be a bilateral mess between hospitals, third-party administrators and insurers under IRDAI; and the DPDP Act, with its consent architecture, has converted patient-data handling from a matter of hospital policy into a matter of statute. For a vendor, each of these is simultaneously a compliance cost and a sales argument.

Outside India, Bunyaad's exposure is concentrated. Bustan Medical Group LLC, a Dubai operator of four hospitals and nineteen clinics across the Emirates, signed in September 2025 for ₹23.4 crore over three years, the largest single contract in the company's history, and carries regulatory obligations to the Dubai Health Authority and the emirate's health information exchange that have no Indian analogue.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

In September 2025 Bustan signed. Dev Menon, negotiating from Singapore at one in the morning, accepted a clause his own legal counsel flagged and his sales colleague described as harmless: where Bunyaad publishes a feature on its public roadmap against a stated quarter, Bustan may treat availability within two quarters of that date as a service expectation, with a service-credit remedy. Everyone in the room understood "availability" to mean the release existing. Nobody asked which date Bustan's compliance team would measure from.

In January 2026 Bunyaad published its first public roadmap page: four items, four quarters, no qualifiers. Vikram wrote it in an afternoon.

Through 2026 the company believed it was executing well. The claims-exchange connector was released to general availability in June, on the published quarter. Internally this was recorded as delivered. In October, Lagan's chief information officer wrote directly to Meenakshi to say that Bunyaad had missed the claims module and that his insurance desk had been staffing the gap manually since July. He was not wrong and neither was the delivery log. The release existed in June; Lagan's change advisory board had scheduled the upgrade for March 2027 across its nineteen facilities.

That letter caused the first real measurement. Joel's team spent December pulling upgrade telemetry across the install base, and in January 2027 produced Exhibit 2, which showed a median lag of forty-one weeks between general availability and a given facility actually running the release, and a ninetieth percentile of sixty-three weeks.

In December 2026, Laukik Capital Partners issued a term sheet for a ₹640 crore Series D, priced against net revenue retention of 118 per cent or better. FY26 retention came in at 109. Laukik's partner, Anuradha Bhagat, did not withdraw; she asked for a product plan that showed how expansion revenue would arrive, and she asked to see it on Monday.

In February 2027 the DPDP consent-manager obligations acquired an operative date. Farida Qureshi's estimate of the work — consent capture, revocation propagation across nineteen downstream modules, audit trail, and per-customer validation — came to 620 engineer-weeks. Total available capacity for the first half of FY28, after support, regressions and the Bustan-specific work, is 2,040 engineer-weeks. The four candidate initiatives in Exhibit 4 sum to 3,180.

5. The people

Dr Meenakshi Rao Co-founder and Chief Executive, Hyderabad Wants one story told identically to the board, the customers and the market. Her instinct as a clinician is that a hospital deserves to be told plainly what is and is not certain. What she is not saying: she needs the Laukik round closed before June, and she has begun to suspect that the 2022 tenancy decision — hers — is the actual constraint, which would make this a very expensive conversation to open in front of an investor.
Joel D'Souza Co-founder and VP Engineering, Pune Wants the public roadmap to carry no dates at all until the upgrade-automation programme exists, and has costed that programme at 1,240 engineer-weeks. What he is not saying: his team has absorbed three consecutive quarters of unplanned regulatory work, two senior engineers resigned in January citing whiplash, and he is using the roadmap argument to protect a capacity argument he has lost twice already.
Farida Qureshi Director, Regulatory & Clinical Safety, Bengaluru Wants consent-manager work stated first and unconditionally, because a hospital compliance officer reading a hedged sentence will assume the vendor is not ready and will begin evaluating alternatives. What she is not saying: her own 620-week estimate has a range she has not published, and the lower bound depends on a legal interpretation that is not yet settled.
Dev Menon Head of Customer Success, Singapore Wants dates, privately and per account, under the existing non-disclosure agreements, rather than in public. What he is not saying: he negotiated the Bustan clause, his team's survey (Exhibit 6) is the optimistic number in the board pack, and the survey's non-response rate is disclosed only in a footnote he wrote himself.
Gregory Almeida Head of Sales, New Jersey Wants the January 2026 format continued — items, quarters, no qualifiers — and points to Exhibit 5, which attributes ₹341 crore of open pipeline to roadmap items. What he is not saying: he has already sent the unpublished FY28 dates to two American prospects, and his variable compensation for the year is weighted to new logos rather than renewals.
Rhea Dalvi Director, Data & AI, Toronto Owns ambient clinical documentation. Wants it on the roadmap as the company's differentiator and is the loudest voice for naming a quarter. What she is not saying: her pilot accuracy is measured on English-language consultations, and forty per cent of consultations in Bunyaad's install base are conducted at least partly in Hindi, Marathi or Telugu.

6. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 is the artefact itself: the three sentences, and what each audience is expected to take from them.

7. Voices

Gregory Almeida to Vikram Sundaresan, email, 2 March 2027"I understand the theology. Here is the practice. The last four US prospects asked for the roadmap in the first call. Lipi hands over a page with quarters on it. If we hand over a page that says 'Next' and 'Later', we are the vendor that would not answer the question. I am not asking you to lie. I am asking you to write down what you already believe."
Joel D'Souza, #leadership channel, 3 March 2027, 07:12 IST"Look at Exhibit 3 before we argue about the page. Sixty-nine per cent of our facilities are not on the current release. Whatever we publish on Friday is a statement about a build, and a build is not a thing our customers have. We are debating the wording of a sentence whose subject does not exist yet."
Farida Qureshi to Vikram Sundaresan, call notes, 4 March 2027"Please do not put a confidence label on the consent manager. A hospital compliance officer is not reading it the way you mean it. If we write 'medium confidence' against a statutory obligation, their legal team will write a memo recommending they evaluate an alternative vendor, and I will spend the next two quarters answering that memo instead of building the thing."
Leena Bhattacharya, design research readout, 26 February 2027"Every CIO we showed the January page to read the quarter and ignored everything around it. One of them had annotated it. Against Q3 he had written, in pen, 'ask for penalty'. We can caveat as carefully as we like. The quarter is what survives the photocopier."

8. The options as Vikram currently frames them

Option A — publish dates, as before. Keep the January 2026 format: named items, named quarters, on the public page, in the board deck and at the advisory board. Gregory gets his instrument, Bhaskar Research scores the transparency criterion, and Rhea gets ambient documentation named with a quarter. The exposure is Exhibit 2: any quarter published becomes, for Bustan, a clock whose start date is now disputed, and for every other customer a date their own change board will not honour, so the company is judged against a promise only it can fail.

Option B — publish outcomes and confidence, no dates. A Now / Next / Later page in plain language, with named dependencies and confidence stated in words, and dates released privately per account under existing agreements. This is what Vikram and Leena believe is honest and what Joel can live with. The exposure is that Farida is probably right about at least one audience: a hedged sentence against a statutory obligation is not read as candour, it is read as unreadiness, and the hospital compliance officer is the one person in this case with the authority to start an evaluation.

Option C — publish two documents. A public outcome roadmap with no dates, plus a contractual availability schedule issued per customer that names the date that customer's own estate will be upgraded, negotiated with that customer's change board. It is the most truthful structure available and it requires someone to own the upgrade path for 310 facilities, which is the 1,240 engineer-weeks in Exhibit 4 that nobody has funded and no customer has requested, and which would have to be taken out of the same 2,040.

Vikram had written these three onto a card. What he had not written, and what Joel had said out loud on Tuesday and been talked past, was that all three options treat the document as the variable. Exhibit 4 contains a fourth item with zero revenue attached to it and no advocate in the room. It is also the only item that would change what any published date actually means.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets at nine on Monday, and Anuradha's term sheet expires on 30 June. The Customer Advisory Board convenes in Mumbai on Tuesday with eleven CIOs, including Lagan's, in the room together for the first time; whatever is said there will be on the phone to the other fifty-one groups by Wednesday. The public page must be live by Friday for Bhaskar Research's window on 19 March.

Capacity for the first half of FY28 is 2,040 engineer-weeks against 3,180 requested, and the hiring plan is frozen until the round closes, which is itself contingent on the retention story the board will hear on Monday. The DPDP consent-manager obligation has an operative date that no commercial decision can move. Bustan's contract carries a two-quarter service expectation whose measurement date is genuinely unsettled, against ₹23.4 crore, with a renewal conversation in June. And the 2022 tenancy architecture, which produced the gap between shipping and delivering, cannot be unwound inside any horizon the roadmap covers.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. What, precisely, did the January 2026 public roadmap page communicate? Separate what it said from what each of the four audiences in Exhibit 1 took away, and identify at what point the two diverged.
  2. Exhibits 2, 3 and 6 describe the same install base and disagree. Which would you take to Tuesday's advisory board, which to Monday's board meeting, and what does the fact that those might be different answers tell you?
  3. Exhibit 5 shows ₹341 crore of pipeline attributed to roadmap items against ₹214 crore of distinct pipeline. How should Vikram use that number in front of Anuradha without either overstating it or discarding it?
  4. Farida and Leena both claim to speak for the customer and reach opposite conclusions about confidence language. What evidence would settle the disagreement, and could it be gathered before Friday?
  5. Joel's contention is that the roadmap is being asked to compensate for an operational gap. If he is right, what should appear on the published page, and who at Bunyaad should be accountable for the gap itself?
  6. What should Vikram do on Monday morning — and what exactly should he say to the board about FY28, knowing that the same words will be read on Tuesday by eleven CIOs and published on Friday to the market?

It was past one when Vikram closed the CAB deck and left the roadmap page open. He had drafted, deleted and redrafted the consent-manager line four times, and the version on screen now read: DPDP consent manager — in build, targeted for availability in FY28 H1. He looked at it for a while. It was true of the build. It was not true of Lagan, or of most of Exhibit 3, and he was no longer sure whether "availability" meant what he had always assumed it meant, or what Bustan's compliance lead would say it meant on Thursday.

Meenakshi's question was still unanswered in the other window. He typed Yes, looked at it, and deleted it. The office in Pune would be awake in four hours, Berlin in five, Toronto not until the afternoon. Outside, the last of the Sunday traffic on the Outer Ring Road had gone quiet.

The Roadmap as Communication

Alignment without promises is the wrong goal. The expert problem is deciding which few promises to make, who is allowed to make them, and what your record entitles you to claim.

1. Two rooms, eleven days apart

On the morning of 4 February 2026, Shalini Kulkarni, chief product officer of Vahani Instruments, stood in a windowless conference room at the company's Coimbatore plant in front of a purchase requisition she did not want to sign. Vahani makes grid-grade energy and power-quality meters — physical devices, roughly the size of a hardback book, that sit in factory substations and distribution transformers and report consumption, harmonics and outage events to a cloud platform Vahani also sells. Revenue for the year to March 2026 would land at about ₹310 crore, seventy per cent of it hardware. The requisition in front of her was for injection-moulding tooling for the enclosure of the next-generation meter: ₹2.6 crore, twenty-two weeks of lead time from the Taiwanese toolmaker, and non-refundable after the first design freeze.

Twenty-two weeks of lead time is a fact about the physical world, not an estimate. If Shalini signed on 4 February, first article samples would arrive in the second week of July and volume production could start in September. If she waited a month to be more certain about the electronics, the whole programme moved a month, the pilot with a large western-India distribution utility slipped past the pre-monsoon site-access window, and the tender Vahani intended to bid for in November would have to be bid with the old meter. Signing meant asserting a date. Not asserting one, in this context, was also asserting a date — a later one, chosen by default rather than by judgement.

What made the room tense was that Vahani had spent the previous eighteen months deliberately removing dates from its roadmap. The programme had been well intentioned and reasonably well executed. The company's software roadmap had been reorganised into confidence horizons; outcome statements had replaced feature names; a revision log was published after every steering review. And yet the November 2025 board pack still carried forty-one lines, the phrase "high confidence" appeared against twenty-nine of them, and when Shalini's chief of staff quietly polled the eight attendees a week later, the mean number of roadmap items any of them could name was 3.1. The format had changed. Whether anything had been communicated was a separate question, and the requisition on the table did not care about horizons.

Eleven days later and 350 kilometres north, Arjun Salvi, head of product at Vachan AI, was in an equally awkward conversation in Bengaluru. Vachan AI builds voice agents that handle collections reminders, delivery coordination and first-line support in nine Indian languages for lenders, logistics firms and retailers. It is four years old, has raised two rounds, and its entire product depends on foundation models it does not own. On 15 February its largest customer, a non-banking financial company with a two-million-account book, asked for a written roadmap commitment: vernacular collections coverage for Bhojpuri and Marathi, in production, by 30 June 2026, with an audit trail acceptable to the customer's own compliance team under the Reserve Bank of India's digital-lending expectations.

Arjun could not honestly promise that. Not because his team was slow, but because the binding variable was not his. Over the previous fourteen months, containment — the share of calls the agent completed without human escalation — had gone from 41 per cent to 66 per cent on Hindi. Of those twenty-five percentage points, eighteen arrived in the two weeks following model releases by his vendors and seven came from Vachan's own retrieval and prompt work. Roughly seventy-two per cent of his product's improvement had been exogenous: it happened to him. A roadmap line that said "Bhojpuri collections agent, Q2" would be a forecast about somebody else's release schedule, dressed as a plan.

Both of these are problems of roadmap communication, and neither is solved by the standard reform. Shalini's problem is that she must make a hard, dated, expensive commitment and needs the rest of the roadmap to stop diluting it. Arjun's problem is that he must make some commitment to a customer who will otherwise walk, and the only thing he controls well enough to promise is not a feature. The argument of this page is that these two problems are the same problem seen from opposite ends, and that the working-level framing — show direction without making a promise — misdescribes it.

The thesis. A roadmap does not let an organisation avoid promises. Organisations run on promises; they cannot coordinate capital, hiring, tooling, channel or contracts without them. What a roadmap does is route promises: every line either creates a claim on future behaviour, transfers one, or extinguishes one. The expert question is therefore not "how do I show direction without promising?" but "what is my promise budget this period, which two or three lines should spend it, who else is authorised to spend it on my behalf, and what does my calibration record entitle me to claim?" Format is downstream of all four.

2. The idea, its history, and the schools that disagree

Define the object precisely. A roadmap, used as a communication artifact, is a structured public statement of a product's intended direction, ordered by priority and qualified by confidence, whose function is to let other people make decisions they could not otherwise make. That last clause is the whole definition. A roadmap is not primarily a record of intent; it is an input to somebody else's choice — a salesperson deciding what to tell an account, an engineering director deciding where to place two new hires, a marketing head deciding when to book media, a customer deciding whether to renew, a board deciding whether the team can be trusted with the next tranche of capital. If no reader's behaviour changes, the roadmap has communicated nothing regardless of how carefully it was written.

A commitment, by contrast, is a statement that transfers risk. When Shalini signs the tooling requisition, ₹2.6 crore of Vahani's money moves from optional to sunk, and the risk of the date being wrong now sits on Vahani's balance sheet rather than in a slide. When a Vachan salesperson writes "June 2026" into a statement of work with a service-credit clause, the risk of being wrong has been transferred to Vachan from the customer, priced at whatever the clause says. Commitments are not bad. They are how organisations buy coordination, and like anything bought, they have a price.

Where the artifact actually comes from

The visual grammar most software roadmaps still use — rows of work against columns of time — descends from production scheduling. Henry Gantt's bar charts, developed around 1910 to 1915 for ordnance and shipbuilding work, were designed for a setting in which the scope of the work was genuinely known in advance and the uncertainty was about sequencing and resource contention. That is a real setting. It is Shalini's tooling problem. It is not the setting of most software work.

The roadmap proper — the word and the layered practice — entered management from corporate R&D. Motorola, under Robert Galvin, developed technology roadmapping through the late 1970s and 1980s, and Charles Willyard and Cheryl McClees described the process in Research Management in 1987. The Cambridge "T-Plan" work of Robert Phaal, Clare Farrukh and David Probert, published around 2001 and 2004, generalised it into a framework with explicitly stacked layers: market pull on top, product in the middle, technology and capability underneath, all plotted against a long time axis. Crucially, in that tradition the time axis was load-bearing precisely because the decisions it supported were capital decisions with multi-year lead times — fab investments, materials programmes, standards participation. The roadmap was a capital-allocation instrument that happened to look like a schedule.

Software product management inherited the picture and discarded the semantics. It kept the grid of features against quarters, dropped the capital-planning logic that made the dates meaningful, and then discovered that the artifact behaved badly: readers treated the columns as commitments because that is what columns of dates have meant since 1915. The agile movement's response after 2001 was largely to reject the artifact rather than repair it, which left a vacuum that project managers filled with Gantt charts anyway. The reform of 2013 to 2018 — confidence horizons in place of calendar columns, outcomes in place of features, an explicit statement that a roadmap is a plan of action rather than a feature list — repaired the artifact for a particular class of company: venture-funded, pure software, selling to buyers who are not procurement departments, with no physical lead times. It is a good reform. Its limits are the subject of this page.

Running alongside that lineage is a second, more quantitative one that most practitioners never encounter. Barry Boehm's 1981 "cone of uncertainty" proposed that estimation error narrows as a project proceeds, and Steve McConnell popularised the picture in the 1990s. Todd Little's 2006 analysis of several hundred projects at Landmark Graphics found that the cone does not narrow nearly as tidily as drawn — uncertainty persists much deeper into delivery than the picture implies. Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky named the planning fallacy in 1979; Bent Flyvbjerg turned the diagnosis into a method, reference-class forecasting, by insisting that a project's schedule be predicted from the distribution of outcomes of similar past projects rather than from a decomposition of the work in front of you. Daniel Vacanti and Troy Magennis carried the same logic into software delivery with throughput-based Monte Carlo forecasting. And Allan Murphy's 1973 decomposition of the Brier score into reliability, resolution and uncertainty gave the field a way to say precisely what a confidence label is worth — a tool almost no product organisation uses on itself, and one we will use on Vachan AI in section 3.

Five schools, and the exact proposition each will and will not sign

The disagreements in this field are usually reported as a style contest between "dates people" and "no-dates people." That is a caricature that hides the real fault line, which is about which variable is held fixed. Every planning school fixes something and lets something else float, and most arguments between competent practitioners are arguments between people whose contexts make different variables fixable.

Table 1. What each school holds fixed, what it lets float, and where it breaks.
SchoolHeld fixedAllowed to floatBreaks when
Programme / Gantt / NPI gate reviewDate and scopeQuality, team size, costScope is genuinely discovered during the work
Horizon (Now / Next / Later)Relative orderDate and scope bothA downstream actor must spend money on a date
Appetite / fixed-time-variable-scopeDate and teamScope, deliberatelyThe scope floor is set by law or by a contract
Outcome roadmapThe problem and its metricSolution, and usually timingThe outcome depends on parties you do not control
Probabilistic forecastingScopeDate, expressed as a distributionReaders collapse the distribution to its optimistic tail

The outcome school will sign the proposition that a roadmap line should name a measurable change in customer or business behaviour and that teams should be handed problems rather than solutions. It will not sign the proposition that product should routinely give sales a dated feature commitment; it regards that as the mechanism by which product organisations become order-takers. Its strongest evidence is the observed correlation between feature-factory operating models and low measured impact per shipped unit of work. Its weakest point, which its critics press hard, is that an outcome is not a schedulable object: a team can commit to attempting a problem, but it cannot commit to a market's response, and putting outcomes on a timeline reimports exactly the false precision the reform set out to kill.

The horizon school will sign the proposition that calendar columns manufacture a precision the underlying knowledge does not support, and that grouping work by confidence is a more honest representation of what the team knows. It will not sign the proposition that the horizon document is sufficient on its own; its serious proponents have always insisted the artifact is a conversation-starter, not a substitute for conversation. Its vulnerability is empirical and organisational rather than logical: in practice horizons degrade into a deniability vocabulary, and we will see exactly how at Varenya Lending Cloud in section 8.

The commitment school — programme management, hardware new-product-introduction gate reviews, enterprise delivery contracts, and the big-room planning ceremonies of scaled agile frameworks — will sign the proposition that an organisation which cannot make dated commitments cannot coordinate anything expensive, and that the honest response to bad dates is better estimation and owned dependencies, not fewer dates. It will not sign that dates are inherently dishonest. Its evidence is Shalini's requisition: twenty-two weeks of tooling lead time, a plant hiring plan, a channel that has to be trained, a tender calendar set by somebody else. Its characteristic failure is confusing the existence of a date with the existence of a plan, and treating the gate review as the moment of truth when the truth was decided months earlier in the estimate.

The probabilistic school will sign the proposition that a date should be a quantile of a distribution derived from the team's own historical record, and that a single-point date without a probability attached is a category error. It will not sign the proposition that the right response to uncertainty is to stop giving dates, which it regards as an abdication: uncertainty is measurable, therefore it should be measured and published. Its evidence is that throughput-based forecasts routinely outperform decomposition-based estimates on the same teams. Its unresolved problem is human: when you publish a range, readers anchor on its optimistic end, so the act of being honest about uncertainty can leave the reader with a more wrong belief than a single conservative date would have.

The ambiguity school is rarely named in product circles but is the oldest of the five. It descends from Richard Cyert and James March's A Behavioral Theory of the Firm (1963), with its concepts of organisational slack, sequential attention to goals, and the quasi-resolution of conflict. It will sign the proposition that a degree of vagueness in a roadmap is functional: it allows a coalition with incompatible preferences to keep working together, defers conflicts that do not need resolving yet, and preserves the option to change course without anyone losing face. It will not sign that clarity is always better. Its evidence is that organisations which force premature precision on genuinely contested priorities tend to resolve the contest politically rather than analytically and then cannot reopen it. Its obvious danger is that functional ambiguity and simple cowardice look identical from the outside, and the people practising the second always describe themselves as practising the first.

3. Mechanics: the promise budget, worked out

What experts actually do, stripped of vocabulary, is manage three quantities: the number of outstanding promises, the accuracy of the confidence attached to each, and the set of people entitled to issue new ones. Each of these has a quantitative treatment. All three are usually left implicit.

3.1 Issuance: the roadmap line is not the promise

The first move an expert makes is to stop analysing the document and start tracing the channels through which its contents become binding. A single roadmap line at Vahani can leave the room through at least five doors, and the doors have wildly different properties. A line minuted at a board meeting is durable, high-status and hard to revise; a line written into a master services agreement is legally enforceable and priced; a line on a customer quarterly-business-review slide is deniable in principle and undeniable in practice; a line copied into a team OKR becomes a performance-management instrument; a line briefed to an industry analyst returns as a published claim the company cannot retract.

Figure 1. The roadmap line is not the promise. The promise is created in the issuance channels, and only three of the five at Vahani required product's signature. When Shalini's team first counted, thirty-one dated claims about the meter programme were live across contracts, minutes, QBR decks and one analyst briefing; product had authored six of them. Everything in the reform literature addresses the box on the left. The organisational problem lives in the middle and the right.

The second-order effect here is the one most teams miss. Reducing the precision of the left-hand box does not reduce the stock on the right. It changes who fills the stock. When product stops publishing dates, the demand for dates does not disappear — account executives, customer success managers and solution architects are still asked "when," still compensated on closing, and still standing in front of a customer with no answer. They will supply one. The organisation's total exposure to dated claims is roughly constant; what varies is whether those claims were authored by someone with access to the dependency graph. A horizon roadmap deployed without issuance control does not reduce risk. It decentralises it to the people least equipped to price it.

Organisations that plan for graceful partial delivery are implicitly assuming an independence that does not hold.

Product is publishing the p80 because at k = 3 anything below p75 destroys credibility in expectation. The correct way to end that argument is not to negotiate the date but to show the reference class and the asymmetry, and then to ask the only question that changes the answer: are we willing to reduce scope enough that the p80 and the p50 converge? That question — fixing the date and floating the scope — is the appetite school's whole contribution, and it is the only move that legitimately compresses a published date without lying.

4. Conditions: six testable claims, applied to both protagonists

The topic's core instruction — show direction without making a promise — is a conditional recommendation masquerading as a universal one. Below are the six conditions under which it holds, each phrased so it can be checked rather than debated, and each applied to Shalini and Arjun.

C1. No downstream actor has to spend irreversibly on the date. The test is concrete: name the largest sum of money, or the largest irreversible act, that someone will commit on the strength of this line, and name the person who commits it. At Vahani the answer is ₹2.6 crore of tooling with a twenty-two-week lead time, plus a plant hiring plan and a tender submission. C1 fails outright for the hardware spine of the roadmap. At Vachan AI the answer is a customer's own compliance and staffing plan — smaller, but not nothing; the NBFC intends to redeploy eleven agents off the collections desk. C1 partially fails.

C2. Scope is genuinely discovered by doing the work. If what "done" means is fixed in advance by physics, a standard or a statute, the horizon framing is not humility but obfuscation: you know what you have to build, and pretending otherwise conceals a schedule problem as a scope problem. Vahani's enclosure must pass IS 16444; the scope is written down by someone else. Vachan's audit trail must satisfy what the customer's compliance team reads into RBI's digital-lending expectations; the scope is partly fixed, partly negotiable. But Vachan's agent quality is entirely discovered — nobody knows in advance what containment rate a given model will reach on Bhojpuri.

C3. The reader has decision latitude. Direction alone is actionable for an engineering director choosing where to hire, or a designer choosing what to research. It is useless to a procurement officer at a state utility who must fill a date field in a tender document. The test: ask the reader what they will do differently tomorrow if they believe the line. If the honest answer is "nothing, I need a date to do anything," then giving them direction is giving them nothing while feeling virtuous about it.

C4. Downstream lead times are shorter than your uncertainty horizon. Marketing can often be mobilised in six weeks; tooling cannot be mobilised in twenty-two. Where the downstream lead time exceeds your ability to forecast, somebody must commit under uncertainty, and the only question is who and with what buffer. This is why hardware organisations build gate reviews: the gate is a scheduled moment for converting uncertainty into commitment, and pretending it can be deferred is how hardware programmes die.

C5. You have a calibration record, and it is published. Confidence language without a hit rate is noise, as Table 2 demonstrated. The test is brutally simple and almost always fails: ask anyone in the room to state, from memory, the share of last year's "Now" items that landed in window. If nobody knows, the team's confidence vocabulary has no exchange rate and its readers are being asked to accept a currency with no central bank.

C6. Issuance is controlled. The roadmap's promise-reducing property only operates if the organisation can actually prevent unauthorised dated claims. The test is an audit of the last twenty signed order forms and the last ten customer QBR decks for feature-specific dates. If dates appear there that product never authored, the roadmap format is decorative; the company is making promises through a channel the format does not touch.

Where the idea is actively misleading is where these conditions fail hardest. Four situations deserve naming. First, a statutory or regulatory deadline: when a rule has an effective date, that date is a fact about the world, and a "Later" label on the compliance work is not honest humility but a governance failure. Second, a sold obligation: once a date sits in an executed contract with a service-credit clause, the roadmap's job is to track it, not to re-describe it as a bet. Third, a coordinated launch where media, channel training and inventory have been booked. And fourth — the most common and least discussed — the case where an organisation's real problem is that it has no strategy and therefore cannot say what it will refuse. Horizon labels are an excellent place to hide that, because a roadmap with forty "Later" items looks like a company with options rather than a company with no opinion.

5. Hard edge cases and what mature companies actually do

The interesting failures happen at organisational seams, where a roadmap written for one audience is read by another whose incentives differ.

Hardware plus software: two commitment classes on one page

Vahani's eventual answer, and the one most mature hardware-software companies converge on regardless of what their process documents say, is to stop pretending the roadmap is homogeneous. Some lines are iron: their dates are purchases, not forecasts, because a payment has been made or a lead time has been entered. Tooling, certification submissions, plant ramp, silicon tape-out, channel inventory. Other lines are glass: firmware features, analytics, cloud dashboards, anything whose scope is discovered and whose delivery can be re-sequenced at low cost. Iron lines get dates, named executive owners and explicit financial exposure. Glass lines get horizons and outcomes. Drawing both on one page, visibly distinguished, is more honest than either treatment applied uniformly — and it forces the conversation that matters, which is whether a given line has been misclassified.

Figure 3. The same company's roadmap occupies more than one quadrant, which is why a single uniform format always fails somebody. Note the top-right quadrant: work that is both irreversible for the reader and genuinely undiscovered in scope. Neither a date nor a horizon is honest there. The only defensible instrument is a gate — a dated commitment to a decision, with published criteria.

AI-native: committing to a gate rather than a feature

Arjun Salvi's situation sits in that top-right quadrant, and his eventual answer generalises to most AI-native products. When the dominant input to your product's quality arrives exogenously, on a schedule set by model vendors, a feature-dated roadmap is a forecast about another company. What remains fully under Vachan's control is threefold: the measurement, the readiness, and the latency of its own response. So Vachan committed to those. The written commitment to the NBFC read, in substance: the Bhojpuri and Marathi evaluation harness and its third-party audit will be in place by 30 April 2026 — a date Vachan controls completely; production release will follow within twenty-one days of the first model that clears a stated gate of word-error rate at or below twelve per cent and containment at or above sixty-two per cent on a two-thousand-call shadow set; and the gate results will be published to the customer monthly whether or not they pass.

That is a real commitment. It is falsifiable, dated where dating is honest, and it transfers exactly the risk Vachan can price and none of the risk it cannot. It also does something subtler: by publishing the gate criteria in advance, Vachan removed its own ability to declare victory on a weak result, which is the form of dishonesty that AI-native roadmaps are most prone to. The customer's compliance head said afterwards that the monthly failing results were more persuasive than a promise would have been, because they demonstrated that the measurement existed.

Two-sided markets: the roadmap changes the thing it describes

Vinimay Exchange, a business-to-business marketplace matching small manufacturers with bulk buyers, illustrates a second-order effect that single-sided products never encounter. In July 2025 Vinimay published a seller-facing roadmap with "instant settlement" in the Later column — an honest, deliberately non-committal placement. Over the following quarter, 340 sellers who had been about to enrol in Vinimay's existing T+2 settlement product did not enrol, choosing to wait for the better thing they had been told was coming. Enrolment in the live product fell by nineteen per cent and the float revenue attached to it fell by about ₹2.1 crore for the quarter.

The roadmap was accurate and it was destructive, because a published roadmap is not a description of a market; it is an intervention in it. The general principle, familiar to anyone who has watched a pre-announcement freeze demand for a current product, is that the correct question before publishing any customer-visible line is not "is this true?" but "what will the reader stop doing if they believe it?" Mature marketplaces handle this by sequencing disclosure by side and by cohort — telling the sellers who would benefit, when the thing is close enough that the waiting cost is small — and by never publishing a Later item that competes with a live revenue line.

Platform teams and the transfer of variance

The organisational seam that causes the most quiet damage is the internal platform. When Vahani's platform group adopted horizons and removed dates from its internal roadmap, it did not remove uncertainty from the system; it moved uncertainty onto four consuming product teams, each of which had its own external commitments and none of which could plan against "Next." Within two quarters, three of the four had built private forks of the over-the-air update layer — roughly eleven person-months of duplicated engineering, discovered only when a security patch had to be applied four times instead of once.

This is the single most reliable diagnostic for a mis-set internal roadmap, and it costs nothing to run: count the forks. A platform team whose consumers have built shadow implementations has failed to communicate, whatever its document looks like. Mature platform organisations therefore do the opposite of what the reform literature suggests — they give internal consumers harder dates than they give anyone else, because internal consumers are the readers with the least slack and the most direct dependency, and because an internal miss is cheap to renegotiate and a fork is expensive to unwind.

Regulated enterprise: the roadmap as an audit artifact

In regulated B2B — lending platforms, health systems, anything touching the Digital Personal Data Protection Act's obligations or a sectoral regulator's circulars — the roadmap acquires a property it has nowhere else: it may be read, later, by someone determining whether the firm was diligent. A bank's procurement pack routinely asks for a dated implementation plan for control features. Refusing to supply one is not a stance on planning philosophy; it is a decision to lose the deal. What mature firms actually do, as distinct from what they say, is maintain a small, separately governed "regulatory commitments" section of the roadmap — dated, legally reviewed, owned by a named executive, and deliberately quarantined from the discretionary roadmap so that the discretionary roadmap can stay genuinely flexible. The quarantine is the trick. Mixing the two is what produces an organisation in which everything is a commitment and therefore nothing is.

6. Ten distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

One: a roadmap does not reduce the number of promises, it relocates them. The tell-tale sign is an organisation loudly proud of its no-dates roadmap whose order forms are thick with delivery dates. An expert, dropped into a new company, does not read the roadmap first; they read the last twenty signed contracts and the last ten customer QBR decks. The obvious reading — that removing dates from the document reduces exposure — is wrong because demand for dates is generated by the buyer and the compensation plan, not by the document, and unsatisfied demand is met by whoever is standing closest to the customer.

Two: the scarce resource is credibility, and it is spent per commitment, not per document. You can tell an expert by what they argue about in a roadmap review. Competent practitioners argue about wording, ordering and which column an item sits in. Experts argue for twenty minutes about whether a particular line should be one of the three that carries a real date, and are indifferent to the phrasing of the other thirty. The obvious reading — that a better-written roadmap communicates better — is wrong because the roadmap's informational value is concentrated almost entirely in its few strong claims, and every weak claim dressed as a strong one taxes the strong ones.

Three: confidence language without a published hit rate is worse than no language. The tell is that nobody in the room can state last year's number. The obvious reading is that hedged language is more honest than a flat date. It is not: an uncalibrated hedge is dishonesty with better manners, and it destroys the informational value of the strong label as well, because a reader who learns that "high confidence" means fifty-four per cent has no way to tell your genuinely confident claims from your habitual ones. The expert response to a calibration audit is never to soften the labels; it is to shrink the bucket until the label becomes true.

Four: the relevant probability is joint, not marginal. The tell is physical — an expert asked how confident they are about a multi-dependency line counts on their fingers before answering, and often says a number lower than anyone in the room expected. The obvious reading is that confidence should track the weakest link. It should not: five links at 0.85 give a joint of 0.44, comfortably below the weakest one. The corollary an expert draws is not "manage dependencies harder" but "have fewer of them," because the arithmetic of conjunction punishes the count far more than it rewards the effort.

Five: a published roadmap is an intervention, not a description. The tell is that an expert's first question about a customer-facing line is what the reader will stop doing. Vinimay's 340 sellers were behaving rationally on accurate information, and the information cost ₹2.1 crore. The obvious reading — that more transparency is always better for trust — is wrong in any market where the reader has a substitute action, because disclosure of a future option is functionally an announcement that the present option is inferior.

Six: removing dates transfers variance to whoever has the least slack. The tell is the fork count. Someone downstream always absorbs the uncertainty you decline to resolve, and it is almost never the most powerful team; it is the smallest, most dependent one, which quietly builds its own version. The obvious reading is that flexibility upstream creates flexibility everywhere. It does the opposite: upstream flexibility is purchased with downstream buffers, and buffers in a dependent team take the form of duplicated work, not spare time.

Seven: "Later" is a disposal mechanism, not a storage unit. The tell is that an expert's revision log contains public deaths — items removed with a stated reason and a named person who asked for them — while a competent practitioner's Later column grows monotonically. The obvious reading is that parking a request is harmless and politically cheap. It is neither: an un-killed item is an un-refused stakeholder, and the cost shows up as the same conversation recurring every quarter, plus a document that no reader believes because they can see it contains things nobody intends to do.

Eight: outcome framing is about problem ownership, not scheduling. The tell is that an expert can name, for any outcome line, at least two genuinely different solutions that would satisfy it, and will cheerfully say that the team might ship either. The obvious reading — that outcome roadmaps are a superior way to schedule work — is a misunderstanding that produces the worst of both worlds: a timeline of outcomes, which commits the team to results it does not control while telling it nothing about what to build. If a line has exactly one possible implementation, calling it an outcome is a relabelling exercise, and an expert will say so.

Nine: the entire value of a revision log lies in its downgrades. The tell is whether items in the log ever move backwards. A log recording only progress and additions is a marketing document; it proves nothing about the author's honesty because it contains no costly signal. The obvious reading is that a change log builds trust by demonstrating diligence. It builds trust only when it demonstrates willingness to publish bad news before being asked, which is the only evidence a reader has that the good news was not filtered.

Ten: the legend must state permissions, not meanings. A competent practitioner's roadmap legend says "Now means scoped, staffed and high confidence." An expert's legend says "if a line is in Now, you may tell a customer we are building it and give a quarter; you may not put a date in a contract without a commitment memo; if it is in Next you may say we intend to build it and may not give any timeframe." The obvious reading is that defining the terms is sufficient. It is not, because the reader's problem is never semantic — it is that they are about to be asked a question by a customer and need to know what they are allowed to say.

One widely repeated stage claim deserves contradicting. It is often said that early-stage companies should not make commitments because everything is uncertain. In practice early-stage companies make the most consequential commitments in the business — to a design partner, to a first enterprise logo, to an investor — and they make them verbally, undocumented, and with no register. The absence of a roadmap does not mean the absence of promises; it means the absence of a record of them. More than one Series A company has discovered at diligence that it had eleven incompatible verbal commitments outstanding to six customers.

8. Three worked examples, one of them a failure

8.1 Vahani Instruments: separating iron from glass

Shalini's redesign, executed between February and May 2026, did four things. It classified every roadmap line as iron or glass using the test in Figure 3, which produced nine iron lines and twenty-seven glass. It reduced the count of live dated claims from thirty-one to six by extinguishing or re-dating the rest in writing — a painful exercise that required the general counsel to read four master agreements and one analyst transcript. It applied the p80 rule from Table 4 to every remaining dated line, which pushed three of the six later by between five and eleven weeks. And it introduced a monthly commitment register review with product, legal and revenue operations in the room.

The results through to the September 2026 quarter: five of the six dated commitments landed in window, against a prior-year rate of eleven of thirty-one. The board pack went from forty-one lines to nine; measured recall a week after the review rose from a mean of 3.1 items to 6.4. Sales cycle length was statistically unchanged, which mattered because the revenue team had predicted it would lengthen. And the tooling requisition, signed on 6 February after two days of argument, produced first articles in the second week of July, one week late, inside a buffer Shalini had published in advance as part of the commitment.

The instructive detail is what did not improve. Engineering estimate accuracy was identical: the reference-class ratio for FY27 initiatives came in at a median of 1.38 against the prior 1.40. Nothing about the redesign made the team faster or more accurate. What changed was the number of claims the company had outstanding and the quantile at which it published them. That distinction — between improving delivery and improving the honesty of what you say about delivery — is the whole subject of this page, and conflating them is the most common way for a roadmap reform to be judged a failure when it did precisely what it was designed to do.

8.2 Vachan AI: committing to the gate

The Vachan commitment described in section 5 was signed on 3 March 2026. The evaluation harness and the third-party audit landed on 27 April, three days early, because that work was entirely internal and therefore genuinely forecastable. The gate was published: word-error rate at or below twelve per cent and containment at or above sixty-two per cent on a two-thousand-call shadow set, measured monthly.

Marathi cleared the gate on the 12 June measurement, at an eleven per cent word-error rate and sixty-four per cent containment, and was in production on 29 June, seventeen days later against a promised twenty-one. Bhojpuri did not clear. The June measurement put it at nineteen per cent word-error rate and forty-three per cent containment, and the July and August measurements, both published to the customer as agreed, showed nineteen and then seventeen per cent. As of mid-September 2026 it has still not shipped.

By the standards of feature-dated roadmapping, this is a miss: a customer asked for two languages by June and received one. By the standards of commitment communication, it is a success, and the customer treated it as one, renewing in August for two years. The reason is that Vachan made three promises it controlled — the harness date, the publication cadence, the twenty-one-day latency — and kept all three, while being explicit from the beginning that the fourth thing was a gate and not a date. The counterfactual is worth stating: had Vachan promised "Bhojpuri by 30 June," it would have missed, and at an enterprise trust asymmetry of five to one, that single miss would have cost more credibility than the Marathi delivery earned.

8.3 Varenya Lending Cloud: the reform that broke a company's quarter

Varenya Lending Cloud sells loan origination and collections software to banks and non-banking financial companies. In January 2025 its then chief product officer, Ishaan Mehra, adopted horizon roadmapping wholesale after a difficult year of missed dates — no dates anywhere, outcomes on every line, a published revision log, exactly the reform as written. It was, by every process measure, well implemented.

Three things went wrong in sequence. First, procurement collided with philosophy: bank technology procurement packs require a dated implementation plan for control and audit-trail features, and Varenya's new answer — a horizon and an outcome statement — was non-responsive. Eleven deals stalled. Approximately ₹18 crore of pipeline moved out by two quarters, which for a company at that stage was most of a year's growth plan.

Second, issuance did not stop, it merely went underground. Two account executives, needing something to say, pulled dates from a superseded October 2024 deck that still sat on the shared drive. Both dates were wrong. Both ended up in executed statements of work with service-credit clauses. Varenya paid ₹46 lakh in credits on those two accounts — money lost not despite the no-dates policy but because of it, since the policy removed the authorised source of dates without removing the demand.

Third, and most corrosive, horizons became a deniability vocabulary. Nothing was in a date-bearing state, so nothing could be late; because nothing was late, nothing was ever forced to a decision; because nothing was forced to a decision, nothing was stopped. Work in progress rose from nine concurrent initiatives to twenty-one. Median initiative age went from seven weeks to nineteen. In three quarters of retrospectives, the number of items formally recorded as having missed their own stated expectation was zero — which the team initially read as evidence the new system was working.

The recovery, begun in October 2025, is instructive precisely because it was not a reversion. Varenya did not go back to dates on everything. It did three things. It created a quarantined regulatory-commitments section with dated, legally reviewed lines owned by a named executive — six per half-year, no more. It built a commitment register reconciled monthly between product, legal and revenue operations, which is the mechanism in the lower half of Figure 1, and the single change that ended unauthorised issuance. And it capped work in progress at eleven, which was the only intervention that restored throughput.

The cost of catching the problem late was roughly three quarters of growth, ₹46 lakh in credits, and the departure of two enterprise account executives who concluded the company could not support an enterprise sale. The early warning sign had been visible in month three: zero items recorded as late. An organisation in which nothing is ever late is not an organisation that has solved delivery. It is an organisation that has stopped measuring.

Two of these deserve elaboration because they are routinely misdiagnosed. Deniability drift is misread as maturity: a team that has stopped being late looks, superficially, like a team that has got better. The distinguishing test is throughput, not punctuality. If nothing is late and median initiative age has doubled, the team has not improved; it has removed the forcing function that used to end work. Calibration rot is misread as optimism, and is therefore treated with exhortations to be more realistic, which never work. It is structural: it comes from admitting more items to the high-confidence bucket than the bucket can support, and the only treatment is arithmetic — count how many items historically landed, and cap admission at that number.

10. Where competent people genuinely disagree

Whether dated commitments belong on a roadmap at all. The anti-date position, at its strongest, is not that dates are impolite but that they are epistemically unjustified for discovered-scope work and that publishing them corrupts prioritisation: once a date exists, the team optimises for the date, which means cutting quality and scope in ways nobody decided. The pro-date position, at its strongest, is that dates are the only mechanism by which an organisation converts intention into coordinated action across functions that cannot read each other's minds, and that the observed pathologies of dated roadmaps are pathologies of bad estimation and unowned dependencies. This disagreement would be settled by evidence on whether organisations that publish few dated commitments coordinate expensive cross-functional work as well as those that publish many, controlling for product type. That evidence does not exist. What is clear is that the anti-date position is close to unarguable for consumer software and close to unusable for hardware, and that most of the heat comes from people generalising from their own quadrant of Figure 3.

Whether ambiguity is a defect or a resource. The behavioural-theory position holds that a roadmap's vagueness is often doing real work — holding a coalition together, deferring a conflict that does not need resolving this quarter, preserving the option to change without anyone losing face. Its evidence is that organisations forced into premature precision on genuinely contested priorities tend to resolve the contest by politics and then find it unreopenable. The opposing position holds that this is a rationalisation for avoidance, and that the costs of ambiguity — Varenya's twenty-one concurrent initiatives — are concrete while its benefits are asserted. For the ambiguity position to be wrong, you would need to show that teams which force early explicit prioritisation produce better outcomes even where stakeholder preferences are genuinely incompatible, not merely where someone lacked the nerve to choose. Nobody has separated those two cases empirically, and from outside they look identical.

Whether to publish a range or a single conservative date. The probabilistic school says publish the distribution; concealing it is paternalistic and loses information. The opposing view accepts the arithmetic and rejects the communication, on the grounds that readers anchor: given "eleven weeks at p50, eighteen at p80," a salesperson will quote eleven, a customer will hear eleven, and the organisation ends up committed to the quantile with the worst expected credibility. On this view, publishing a single p80 date and holding the distribution internally produces more accurate beliefs in readers' heads than publishing the true distribution does. This is testable and rarely tested; the measurement is simply to see which number appears in the next twenty customer emails. Where it has been informally tested, the anchoring worry appears justified, which is uncomfortable for anyone who believes transparency is costless.

Whether outcome roadmaps are a discipline or a category error. The critic's strongest form is worth stating properly: a team cannot commit to an outcome, because outcomes depend on customer behaviour, competitor action and market conditions that the team does not control; putting outcomes on a roadmap therefore commits the team to something it cannot deliver while telling nobody what will actually be built, which is strictly worse than a feature list on both axes. The defender's answer is that outcome lines are not commitments but assignments of problem ownership, and that the confusion arises only when outcomes are placed on a time axis. Both are right about something, and the disagreement usually dissolves on inspection into a disagreement about whether a roadmap's rows are promises or briefs.

Whether roadmapping survives exogenous capability. The strong AI-native position is that in a regime where most capability improvement arrives from vendors, a roadmap beyond the current cycle is fiction and the correct artifact is a readiness posture — evaluation infrastructure, gates, and a published response latency, as at Vachan. The strong counter-position is that this is temporary: capability arrival rates will become more predictable, product differentiation will shift back to things teams build themselves, and firms that abandoned medium-term planning will find themselves without the muscle. What would settle it is the variance of vendor capability arrival over the next several years, which nobody can currently forecast — including the vendors.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has studied this topic writes a better roadmap. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in four visible ways.

They treat the number of outstanding dated claims as a managed quantity with a target, and they know what it currently is. Asked "how many live dated commitments does this company have?", they answer with a number, not a shrug, because they have counted. This alone distinguishes perhaps one product leader in ten.

They spend their political capital on issuance control rather than on document design. The hard, unglamorous work of getting revenue operations and legal into a monthly reconciliation, of establishing that a date in a contract requires a commitment memo, of removing a superseded deck from a shared drive — this is what actually moves the exposure, and an expert will do it in preference to another redesign of the artifact, even though the redesign is more visible and much more pleasant.

They are comfortable making hard, dated, expensive promises, and they make few of them. The distinguishing behaviour is not reluctance to commit but discrimination about where. Shalini signed a ₹2.6 crore requisition and simultaneously killed twenty-five of thirty-one dated claims; those are the same act, not opposite ones. A leader who cannot commit is as broken as one who commits to everything, and the second failure is at least legible.

And they keep score on themselves in public. They know their reference-class ratio, their calibration by bucket, and their on-time rate, and they say those numbers out loud to the board before anyone asks. The paradox, repeatedly observed, is that publishing an unflattering hit rate increases trust more than a flattering roadmap does, because it is the only costly signal available in a domain where anyone can write anything on a slide.

12. What each protagonist decides

Shalini Kulkarni signed the tooling requisition on 6 February 2026, two days after the meeting, having done exactly one piece of work in between: she made her team compute the joint probability in Table 3 and then removed the field-access dependency from the critical path by restructuring the pilot so that the first fifty meters could be commissioned at a Vahani-controlled test substation rather than at the utility's site. That single change took the joint from 0.40 to 0.54, and more importantly it moved the riskiest link from a party Vahani could not influence to one it could. Her reasoning, as she put it to the board, was that the date was going to be asserted either way — by her in February or by default in March — and that the only thing she could actually improve was the number of external hands the date passed through. She then spent April and May extinguishing twenty-five dated claims, which she later described as the harder and more valuable half of the work.

Arjun Salvi refused the customer's requested commitment on 20 February and offered the gate structure instead, having first run the calibration audit in Table 2 and shown it to his own chief executive, who had until then believed the roadmap was in good shape. His reasoning was that the NBFC's real requirement was not a date but the ability to plan a staffing change with some assurance, and that a published gate with a twenty-one-day response commitment gave them a better basis for that than a date he expected to miss with probability one half. The customer accepted after eight days and one escalation. Marathi shipped; Bhojpuri has not; the account renewed.

Discussion questions

  1. Vachan AI kept every promise it made and did not deliver the capability the customer asked for; Varenya Lending Cloud made no promises at all and paid ₹46 lakh in service credits. If the stock of outstanding promises is roughly conserved regardless of roadmap format, what does that imply about where a product leader's first ninety days of effort should go — and what would you expect to see get worse before it gets better?
  2. The break-even calculation in Table 4 says the minimum honest publishable confidence is k/(1+k), where k is the ratio of credibility lost per miss to credibility gained per hit. Is k a property of the organisation, of the relationship, or of the individual leader's history? If a new product leader inherits a team with a poor record, does k transfer to them — and if so, is the correct response to publish later dates or to make fewer commitments?
  3. Shalini separated her roadmap into iron and glass and defended it as more honest than a uniform format. A critic could argue that this simply gives the organisation two roadmaps, reimports the Gantt chart under a new name for the half that matters most, and leaves the discretionary half to be quietly deprioritised. Which of these two readings is right depends on what evidence — and how would you collect it inside a company in a single quarter?

13. Going deeper

  • Roadmaps: Now / Next / Later. The format this page has been arguing with. Worth revisiting specifically to see which of its claims survive the calibration audit and which are conditional on a pure-software, low-lead-time context. Unlocks: the ability to deploy horizons where they work and refuse them where they do not.
  • Communicating with leadership. Boards and executives are the audience with the highest trust asymmetry and the shortest attention, which makes them the hardest test of everything here. Unlocks: the practice of publishing your own hit rate before being asked.
  • Customer-facing roadmaps. The external view is where issuance risk and the reflexivity problem from Vinimay Exchange both become acute, because the reader can act on the information in ways that change your market. Unlocks: disclosure sequencing by side and cohort.
  • Commitment levels and confidence language. The direct continuation: a vocabulary of committed, planned, exploring and shelved is only as good as the calibration behind it, and this topic supplies the exchange rate. Unlocks: contracts and QBR decks that say what the roadmap meant.
  • Strategy vs roadmap vs plan. The roadmap becomes a strategy substitute whenever the strategy is weak, and the tell is a roadmap that changes while the strategy document has not been touched in eighteen months. Unlocks: the ability to say what the company will refuse.
  • OKRs and goal setting. The mechanism by which roadmap lines become performance commitments for individuals, which is the issuance channel with the strongest incentive to distort. Unlocks: an understanding of why teams sandbag key results and why that is rational.
  • Annual and quarterly planning. The cadence at which the promise budget is actually set and reconciled; the commitment register review in Figure 1 belongs inside this rhythm rather than beside it. Unlocks: planning that produces decisions rather than documents.
  • Capacity planning. The constraint that determines how many items the Now bucket can honestly hold — the arithmetic behind Vachan's cap of roughly two per quarter. Unlocks: a defensible answer to “why can’t we do all of it?”
  • Dependency management. The conjunction arithmetic in Table 3 argues for fewer dependencies rather than better-managed ones; this topic covers what to do when you cannot reduce the count. Unlocks: critical-path restructuring of the kind Shalini used to move the riskiest link in-house.
  • Milestones and release planning. Where iron lines actually get delivered, and where the gate reviews that hardware and regulated software depend on are designed. Unlocks: the discipline of converting uncertainty into commitment at a scheduled moment rather than continuously.
