The Roadmap as Communication

How to show direction without making a promise you cannot keep.

1. A slide, an hour before the board

It is the second week of August 2026, and Meera Iyer, vice-president of product at Olakh Systems, is sitting alone in a glass-walled meeting room on the fourth floor of the company's Bangalore office, rereading a slide she has already read six times. Olakh Systems is a nine-year-old business selling workflow-automation software to mid-market manufacturers — the kind of company that runs approvals, quality checks and vendor onboarding through Olakh's platform instead of paper files and email chains. Annual recurring revenue sits at roughly ₹42 crore, growing but not fast enough to be comfortable, and in forty minutes Meera has to walk the board through the second-half roadmap. One line on the slide reads, simply, "Approvals Workflow 2.0 — Q4."

The line matters more than its brevity suggests. A Pune-based auto-components manufacturer, one of Olakh's five largest accounts, was told nine months ago that a compliance-grade approvals workflow was "coming soon." It did not come soon. The account's renewal is due in November, and the customer's operations head has said, in writing, that a further slip will end the relationship. Separately, Olakh's VP of sales wants a firm date because two new anchor deals worth roughly ₹3.1 crore in combined first-year value are sitting in the pipeline, both asking for the same capability before they will sign. And the engineering lead has just told Meera, an hour before the board call, that the compliance layer depends on an audit-log service that is not yet built, which itself depends on a data-retention vendor contract that legal has not yet signed.

Meera's dilemma is not really about the feature. It is about what a single line on a roadmap slide is allowed to mean. If she gives the board and the sales team a hard date, and it slips again — as it already has once — the story that reaches Olakh's next fundraising conversation, already softened by a weak first quarter, becomes "the product team promised this before and missed it twice." If she refuses to commit to anything at all, the board, led by a director from a Mumbai private-equity fund that holds a 22 percent stake and has seen tidy Gantt charts from Olakh's sister portfolio companies, will read her caution as evidence that product management has no plan. She needs a way to tell the room exactly where the company is headed and in what order, precise enough that sales can shape what it tells the Pune customer and engineering can sequence its work, without the line on the slide quietly becoming a contract that nobody signed but everybody will hold her to.

2. The idea: a map, not a manifest

The discipline Meera needs a name for is roadmap communication — the practice of using a roadmap to align an organisation on direction and relative priority without implying a delivery promise the team cannot honestly make. A roadmap, in this sense, is a communication artifact: a shared picture of where a product is headed and why, sequenced by how confident the team is in each piece of that picture, not a calendar of dates the team is contractually bound to hit.

The problem this idea was invented to solve is a specific and recurring one. Through the 2000s and into the early 2010s, most product roadmaps borrowed their format from programme-management Gantt charts: a grid of features against calendar quarters, presented to executives and often to customers as a plan. Because the format looked precise, everyone treated it as a promise — sales quoted the dates in contracts, customers built their own plans around them, and when engineering reality inevitably diverged from the chart, as it does on almost any nontrivial piece of software, the roadmap's failure to hold became a trust problem rather than an ordinary planning adjustment. Janna Bastow, co-founder of the roadmapping tool ProdPad, popularised an alternative around 2013 and 2014: the "Now / Next / Later" roadmap, which replaced calendar columns with confidence horizons. C. Todd Lombardo, Bruce McCarthy, Evan Ryan and Michael Connors formalised the underlying argument in their 2017 book "Product Roadmaps Relaunched," writing that a roadmap is a plan of action to achieve a goal, not a list of features with dates attached to them. Around the same period, voices including Melissa Perri pushed the idea further into "outcome roadmaps," where each line names a measurable change in customer or business behaviour rather than a feature to be shipped, with objectives and key results, OKRs, providing the link between the roadmap and company strategy.

The sentence Meera can say in the boardroom without sounding evasive, and without sounding glib, is this: this roadmap shows you where we are headed and in what order, not when we will arrive. It is not a hedge. It is a precise description of what the artifact is for.

3. How it actually works

Converting a feature list into a roadmap that communicates rather than promises involves a specific sequence of moves, several of which experienced practitioners perform automatically and therefore never write down for anyone learning the discipline for the first time.

The first move is to sort every initiative into a confidence horizon rather than a calendar slot. "Now" means the work is scoped, staffed and close enough to committed that the team would be surprised, not merely disappointed, if it slipped. "Next" means the direction is set and resourcing is likely, but scope and sequencing inside the next one or two quarters can still move. "Later" means a directional bet under investigation, which may not happen at all in its current form. The horizon is a confidence bucket, not a hidden calendar with the labels painted over.

The second move is to say the confidence out loud on the artifact itself, not just imply it through which column an item sits in. A line in "Next" should carry a phrase like "likely, pending scoping" rather than relying on the reader to remember what "Next" means in the abstract.

The third move is to anchor each line to an outcome, not only a feature name. "Reduce approval cycle time from 5.4 days to under 2 days for enterprise accounts" tells the reader what changes in the world; "Approvals Workflow 2.0" tells them only what engineering intends to build, which is a much weaker basis for anyone else in the room to make a decision.

The fourth move, and the one most often skipped, is to put dependencies and risks on the same page as the plan rather than leaving them in an engineering ticket system nobody outside engineering reads. A roadmap that shows "blocked on vendor contract for audit-log service" builds more trust over a year than a clean chart that turns out, on inspection, to have been fictional the whole time.

The fifth move is to build more than one view from a single shared source of truth: an engineering view carrying full dependency detail, an executive view organised by outcome and confidence, and — for a later topic in this sequence — a customer-facing view organised by theme with no dates at all. The figure below shows how one underlying roadmap branches into those views rather than existing as three separately maintained documents that inevitably drift apart.

Figure 1. Three audiences read three different views, but all three are generated from the same underlying set of horizons and confidence labels — so a change made once is seen consistently everywhere, instead of three documents drifting apart.

The sixth move is to set a revision cadence and say it aloud: "this is the picture as of August 11; we revisit at the September steering review." That single sentence converts a future change from a broken promise into an expected event. The seventh is to answer "when does this ship" by translating the question into the decision the asker is actually trying to make — should sales quote a date to a customer, should engineering begin work now — rather than manufacturing a date whose only purpose is to end the conversation. And the eighth move, the one most consistently left implicit, is to write down explicitly, for anything sitting in "Now," what would have to remain true for that placement to hold — "if the audit-log vendor contract closes by 20 August" — because a stated assumption is a visible risk, while an unstated one is a landmine.

4. A worked example: scoring, then re-scoring, Olakh's second half

Meera's team scores its candidate initiatives with a RICE framework — Reach, Impact, Confidence and Effort — before deciding which horizon each belongs in. Reach is the number of accounts the initiative touches per quarter. Impact is scored on a fixed scale: 3 for massive, 2 for high, 1 for medium, 0.5 for low, 0.25 for minimal. Confidence is a percentage reflecting how sure the team is in its own Reach and Impact estimates. Effort is measured in person-months of engineering time. The score is Reach multiplied by Impact multiplied by Confidence, divided by Effort.

5. Nuances a learner must sit with

A roadmap is neither a backlog nor a project plan

A backlog is an ordered list of work items at a level of detail suitable for a sprint; a project plan sequences tasks with dependencies at a level of detail suitable for a delivery manager. A roadmap sits above both, communicating direction to people who need to make decisions, not to execute tasks. Collapsing the three into one document usually produces something too detailed to read quickly and too vague to build from.

No dates does not mean no accountability

The "Now" horizon still carries a working target and a named owner; it is qualified by an explicit assumption, not stripped of responsibility. Teams that use the horizon format as cover for vagueness have misunderstood it as thoroughly as teams that use hard dates as cover for false certainty.

Confidence language must be calibrated, not vibes-based

If items labelled "likely" in fact ship on time only four times out of ten, the label is dishonest regardless of how humble it sounds. Calibration means checking, periodically, what percentage of past "Now" items actually landed within the stated window, and adjusting the language the team uses accordingly.

A roadmap is a hypothesis about outcomes, not proof of them

Even a perfectly communicated roadmap for "reduce approval cycle time" does not guarantee the outcome, because the outcome also depends on customers actually adopting the new workflow, which Olakh does not fully control. Communicating a plan well and being right about the underlying strategy are two separate achievements, and a reader should never assume the first implies the second.

It is routinely confused with three other artifacts

A commitment, a strategy, and a prioritised backlog all resemble a roadmap because they can all be drawn as a list of rows in rough order. A roadmap borrows structure from all three without being any of them, which is precisely why people who have not thought carefully about the distinction tend to use the word "roadmap" for whichever of the three they happen to be holding.

It cannot rescue a wrong strategic bet

However cleanly Meera communicates the direction, if Approvals Workflow 2.0 solves a problem the market has already moved past, good communication only makes the failure legible sooner. The roadmap format improves trust in the process; it does not improve the quality of the underlying decision.

Audience literacy has to be taught, not assumed

A board accustomed to Gantt charts from other portfolio companies may read a horizon roadmap as evasive unless someone explains, once and explicitly, what each horizon licenses the reader to assume and to say to a customer. The format change requires a short translation the first time it is used with any new audience.

Revision must happen in public

Quietly sliding an item from "Now" to "Next" without flagging the move recreates exactly the trust problem the horizon format exists to prevent. A visible revision log — one paragraph, dated, explaining what changed and why — is not optional overhead; it is the mechanism that makes the whole approach credible over more than one quarter.

6. How this differs by product type and company stage

In a consumer product, the roadmap's primary audience is usually internal — growth and marketing teams, not external contract-signers — and it tends to be organised around funnel and cohort metrics rather than named accounts. A consumer wellness app such as Onima Fit might build its roadmap around a single retention curve: initiatives are sequenced by their expected effect on day-30 retention for a specific cohort, and the absence of an external customer demanding a date changes the pressure on the format, though not the underlying discipline.

In a B2B product like Olakh, the roadmap doubles as a sales-enablement and renewal-defence document, which is precisely what makes Meera's problem harder than a purely internal planning exercise: account-specific promises leak out of internal slides and into order forms with "will deliver by" clauses that legal has to negotiate around. The added communication burden in B2B is training sales and customer success on exactly what each horizon licenses them to tell a customer, because the roadmap's audience now includes people who are contractually binding the company based on what they believe it says.

In a marketplace, the roadmap has to satisfy two sides that often want opposite things. A marketplace such as Ozar Bazaar has to communicate direction to sellers, who want inventory and payout tooling, and to buyers, who want faster discovery and cheaper delivery, and a roadmap review in that setting frequently becomes an internal negotiation between two constituencies before it becomes a document either side sees.

Company stage changes the format's usefulness in its own way. At an early-stage startup of a dozen people, the roadmap is often communicated verbally in a weekly all-hands, because the entire company can absorb a change in direction directly and a formal horizon-labelled document can slow trust-building rather than help it. At a company the size Olakh has become, roughly three hundred people across several business units, the roadmap is frequently the only channel through which most of the organisation learns the direction at all, which is exactly why its absence, or its ambiguity, becomes far more expensive at scale than it ever was in the twelve-person version of the same company.

7. Common mistakes

Sales quotes a horizon label as a hidden date. The symptom is a signed order form containing a specific ship date that never appeared in any product commitment memo. The underlying misunderstanding is treating "Now" as a calendar date with the numbers filed off rather than as a confidence bucket. The cheapest diagnostic is a quarterly audit of signed contracts for feature-specific dates; if any appear that product never authorised, the roadmap is functioning as a contract regardless of what its authors intended.

Engineers treat the roadmap review as a formality. The symptom is a team that shows up to roadmap reviews saying "we already know what we're building," with no real discussion. The underlying misunderstanding is reading the roadmap as a status report of a plan engineering has already fixed, rather than as a two-way negotiation surface where priorities can genuinely move. The diagnostic is to ask when an item last changed horizon because of pushback from someone outside engineering; if the answer is never, the roadmap review is a rubber stamp.

The roadmap looks suspiciously stable. The symptom is a document that reads almost identically quarter after quarter. The underlying misunderstanding is treating the absence of visible change as evidence of a stable strategy, when it more often means nobody is actually updating a shared artifact and it has quietly diverged from reality. The diagnostic is to pick three items that were in "Now" three months ago and check their real status; a wide, undocumented gap reveals a stale document being mistaken for a living one.

Leadership reverts to demanding a Gantt chart. The symptom is a board or executive team complaining that the roadmap "has no dates, so I can't plan around it," and asking for the old format back. The underlying misunderstanding is that horizon language was introduced without ever training the audience on what decision each label actually licenses them to make. The diagnostic is to ask a roadmap reader to state, in their own words, what they are and are not allowed to promise a customer based on a specific line; an inability to answer means the format was deployed without the translation step it needs.

8. What good looks like

Meera opens the board review not with the roadmap itself but with one sentence describing the format: "Now means scoped, staffed and high confidence; Next means the direction is set but sequencing can still move; Later means a bet we're actively investigating." Only after that does she show the RICE table, and when she reaches Approvals Workflow 2.0 she says out loud that she is overriding the pure score, names the reason — retention risk on the Pune account and two pipeline deals worth ₹3.1 crore — and states the single assumption that keeps the item in "Now": that the audit-log vendor contract closes by 20 August. She hands the private-equity director a one-page dependency view that names the vendor blocker in plain language instead of folding it into a generic "in progress" bar that would have hidden the real risk. The sales VP leaves the room able to tell the Pune customer something specific and honest: compliance capability targeted for the fourth quarter, contingent on a vendor step Olakh is actively closing — precise enough to hold the account's patience, honest enough to survive a delay if one occurs. When the vendor contract signs two days late, nobody owes anyone an apology tour, because the assumption behind the date, and the risk to it, was named in the room three weeks earlier.

9. What Meera decides, and what to learn next

Meera commits Olakh to a horizon-based, outcome-anchored roadmap as the company's single source of truth, with a one-page revision log published after every steering review and a short briefing for sales and customer success on exactly what each horizon licenses them to say to a customer. Her reasoning is straightforward once stated: the cost of continuing to let the roadmap function as an implicit contract — churn risk on a marquee account, and a fundraising narrative weakened by a second missed promise — now exceeds the discomfort of a board that is, for one meeting, unused to a document without dates on it.

The natural next topic is commitment levels and confidence language, because the horizon format removes the false certainty of a calendar date but does not yet give Meera a shared vocabulary — committed, planned, exploring, shelved — for stating precisely how firm any single line really is; that is the next layer of precision the same underlying problem demands. The other natural next step is customer-facing roadmaps, because the external, even-further-stripped-down view Olakh will eventually need to show the Pune account and its own prospects only becomes credible once the internal version underneath it is built correctly, rather than being a cosmetic document invented for outside eyes alone.

Two questions worth sitting with.

When a stakeholder demands a date the team cannot honestly give, is naming the single assumption that would make that date true a genuine alternative to promising it — or is it simply a more sophisticated way of making the same promise, dressed in the language of risk disclosure?

If a company's sales culture already treats every roadmap line as a de facto contract no matter what labels the product team attaches to it, is the fix a better roadmap format at all, or a harder conversation about how sales compensation and customer commitments are actually made?

The Roadmap as Communication

Ishara Fleet Cloud and the Hausla renewal · Gurugram, 12 November 2026

Ritika Deshmukh, vice-president of product at Ishara Fleet Cloud, read the calendar invite from her customer-success lead for the third time. Joint QBR – Hausla Logistics DMCC – renewal discussion. It sat nine days out, on a Saturday afternoon Dubai time that Priya Krishnan had negotiated from Singapore because it was the only slot Hausla's chief operating officer, Yusuf Al Marri, would give before his board met. On that call Ritika would present Ishara's roadmap for the next two quarters. Somewhere in that deck, Rob Castellano, Ishara's sales head, wanted a sentence that did not yet exist: a ship date for predictive dispatch, written plainly enough that legal could drop it into the renewal as a service commitment. Ritika's engineering lead in Bengaluru and her data scientist in Toronto both told her, independently, that the sentence would be a lie. She had nine days to decide what the roadmap slide would actually say.

Company background

Ishara Fleet Cloud was founded in Gurugram in 2016 to solve a problem every logistics operator in India recognised: fleets were tracked on paper and phone calls while customers wanted an ETA accurate to the minute. Its software ingests telematics and driver-app pings, optimises dispatch across a depot's vehicles, and gives operations managers and their customers a live, defensible delivery promise. By FY26 it had grown to roughly ₹96 crore in annual recurring revenue and 340 employees, competing for logistics and quick-commerce accounts against FarEye and LogiNext at home and a scatter of regional players in the Gulf. Its engineering base sits in Bengaluru and Pune; product design runs out of a small Berlin studio Ishara acquired in 2023; and a two-person data-science team, led out of Toronto, builds the machine-learning models that increasingly differentiate the product from cheaper dispatch tools. Hausla Logistics DMCC, a Dubai-based freight and last-mile operator running fleets across the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Egypt, is Ishara's largest account outside India: ₹14.6 crore in annual contract value, up for a three-year renewal.

The situation

Hausla's renewal is not in doubt on price. What is in doubt is trust. Eighteen months earlier, Ishara had told Hausla's operations team that "dynamic driver-allocation" — a feature that reassigns undelivered stops in real time — would ship in the first quarter of 2026. It shipped ten weeks late, after a telematics data-quality problem in Bengaluru's test fleet turned out to affect nearly a third of Hausla's older vehicles too. Yusuf Al Marri has since asked, at every call, for the next big feature — predictive dispatch, which forecasts congestion and driver fatigue instead of reacting to them — to come with a hard date this time, "in writing." From Toronto, Aisha Bello, the data scientist building predictive dispatch, tells Ritika the model's backtested ETA accuracy sits at 71 percent against a 90 percent target, and that closing that gap depends on a second and possibly a third quarter of live driving data she cannot compress by adding people. From Bengaluru, Karan Sable, who ships whatever Aisha's model produces, is candid that promising a date before the model clears its accuracy bar simply moves the slip from engineering's calendar to his.

The people

Karan Sable

Head of Engineering, Bengaluru
Wants the roadmap to state ranges and dependencies honestly; is the one who absorbs the cost, in overtime and credibility, of dates that turn out to be wrong.

Aisha Bello

Data Scientist, Toronto
Wants predictive dispatch judged by its accuracy bar, not a calendar date; worried that a fixed ship date will pressure her into shipping a model that isn't ready.

Rob Castellano

Head of Sales, New Jersey
Wants a written commitment he can put in the renewal; his quarter's number depends on Hausla renewing at the higher three-year tier.

Yusuf Al Marri

Chief Operating Officer, Hausla Logistics DMCC, Dubai
Wants certainty after last year's slip; is evaluating FarEye as a hedge and will read any vague language as evasion.

Exhibits

Exhibit 1 shows why Yusuf no longer accepts a verbal timeline. Of Ishara's last four roadmap commitments made to enterprise clients, three slipped, and the two features that slipped by more than eight weeks were the two Hausla depended on operationally.

Exhibit 2 is the draft roadmap Ritika must decide how to present. The "Now" row is nearly certain; the dispute is entirely about how — and whether — to describe the "Next" row to a client.

Exhibit 2 — Draft H1 2027 roadmap, as prepared for the QBR

Exhibit 3 puts the choice in money. Hausla is ₹14.6 crore of Ishara's ₹96 crore ARR — too large to lose, but the two clients Ishara already lost to broken date promises in FY26 cost it ₹6.2 crore combined, less than half of what one mishandled renewal at Hausla's scale could cost on its own.

The options

  1. Commit to a date. Tell Yusuf predictive dispatch reaches 90% accuracy by 30 April 2027 and let legal write it into the renewal. This is the sentence Rob wants and the fastest path to a signature. Its cost sits with Karan and Aisha: if the second quarter of driving data doesn't close the accuracy gap, Ishara is back where it was eighteen months ago, only this time the miss is contractual, with penalty clauses attached.
  2. Offer outcomes, not dates. Present Exhibit 2 as drafted — Now/Next/Later, with confidence language and named dependencies, and no date on predictive dispatch at all. This protects engineering and data science from a commitment they cannot control, but Rob is likely right that Yusuf's board, burned once already, will read "medium confidence" as the same evasion that cost trust last year, and may accelerate the FarEye evaluation instead of renewing.
  3. Commit to a checkpoint, not a ship date. Promise a firm, small "Now" deliverable (the fatigue-alert overlay, achievable with no open dependencies) inside 60 days, and for predictive dispatch commit to a joint accuracy review with Hausla at the end of Q1 2027 — a date Ishara controls — where the model's measured accuracy, not a promise, decides the next step together. This gives Yusuf something verifiable sooner than a distant ship date, and gives Ishara a recommitment point instead of a single bet, at the cost of a slightly more complex renewal clause that sales will need to learn to sell.

Questions for discussion

  1. What did Ishara's past four roadmap commitments (Exhibit 1) actually communicate to a client — a plan, or a promise? What is the difference?
  2. Whose risk does each of the three options move, and onto whom? Trace what happens to Karan and Aisha under Option 1 if the accuracy gap does not close on schedule.
  3. Is Option 2's confidence language actually more honest than Option 1's date, or only more comfortable for Ishara to say? How would you test that from Yusuf's seat in Dubai?
  4. What would make Option 3's Q1 2027 review a credible checkpoint rather than just a deferred version of the same argument the QBR is trying to close?

A note for the learner

The topic behind this case is simple to state and easy to get backwards in the room: a roadmap's job is to align people on direction, not to bind the organisation to a date. The instinct under client pressure, visible in Rob's position, is to treat vagueness as the risk and a date as the fix. Exhibit 1 shows the opposite is closer to true at Ishara — three of four dates already failed, and the failures did more damage to trust than a well-explained "medium confidence" ever would have. The learning objective is to align people without making a promise the organisation cannot keep.

A well-reasoned answer does three things. It separates what is nearly certain (the Now row, which Ritika can commit to plainly) from what is genuinely uncertain (predictive dispatch's accuracy, which depends on data Ishara does not yet have) and refuses to flatten that difference into one confident-sounding sentence. It gives the anxious party — here, Yusuf, after a real prior miss — something concrete and near-term rather than only a caveat, because confidence language alone reads as stalling to someone already burned. And it converts the far-out uncertainty into a specific, dated mechanism for revisiting the decision, so "we don't know yet" comes with a plan for when they will know, not just a hedge.

On that basis, Option 3 is the defensible path. It gives Rob a near-term deliverable he can announce this quarter, gives Karan and Aisha a commitment they can actually keep, and gives Yusuf a dated review that is itself a promise Ishara controls — unlike a ship date that depends on data nobody has collected yet. Option 1 trades a short-term signature for a repeat of the exact failure Exhibit 1 already shows costs more than it saves. The roadmap Ritika takes into the QBR should say plainly what Ishara knows, what it does not, and exactly when that will change — which is what a roadmap can promise, even when a date cannot.
